A roster is an official list of people who belong to a group, team, or organization — often including extra details like their roles, assigned duties, or scheduled times. The simplest way to think of it: the official roll call of a group.
The word is used in two closely related ways:
1. A list of members — who belongs to the group

This is the most common use today, especially in sports. The roster is the official list of players on a team. If your name is on the roster, you are officially part of that team. If you are removed from the team, you are taken off the roster.

"The cricket team's roster has 20 players this season."
2. A duty or work schedule — who does what, and when

In workplaces, the military, schools, and organizations, a roster is a schedule that assigns duties to people — often in rotation, so the work is shared fairly over time.

"The hospital made a roster showing which nurses work the night shift each week."

This version is often called a duty roster or work roster.
What makes a roster different from just a "list"

An ordinary list can be anything — a shopping list, a list of ideas. A roster is more specific:

  • It always involves people, not objects or things.
  • It is formal and official — created by a team, company, school, or institution.
  • It carries organizational purpose — it tells you who belongs to something, or who is responsible for something.

• "On the roster" — being an official, active member of a group or team.

"She was finally put on the roster after months of training."

  • "Off the roster" / "dropped from the roster" — removed from a team or organization.

"He was dropped from the roster after the injury."

  • "Active roster" — especially in professional sports, this refers to the players currently eligible to play, as opposed to those who are injured or suspended.

"The team's active roster was reduced to 23 players."

  • "Duty roster" — a rotation schedule assigning specific duties to specific people.

"According to the duty roster, it's your turn to close the shop tonight."

  • "Call the roster" — to read all names aloud from the list to check who is present (also called "calling roll" or "roll call").

Roster vs. list: Every roster is a list, but not every list is a roster. A roster is specifically formal, specifically about people, and specifically tied to a group or organization.

Roster vs. schedule: A schedule is about time — what happens when. A roster is about people — who belongs or who does what. A duty roster blends both: it tells you which person is assigned to which time slot.

Roster vs. lineup: A lineup is the specific group chosen to play or perform right now, today, at this moment. A roster is everyone officially on the team — not all of them will necessarily be in the lineup on a given day. Think of the roster as the full pool, and the lineup as the selection made from that pool.

Roster vs. register: A register is usually a permanent or long-term record (like a birth register or a school register that stays fixed). A roster is more dynamic — people are added or removed as the group changes over a season, a project, or a job.
The key idea to carry with you

Whenever you see or hear the word roster, think: an official list of people connected to a group — either showing who belongs to it, or who is responsible for what within it.

If it's a sports context → it's the team's official list of players.
If it's a workplace or institutional context → it's most likely a duty schedule.

Both uses share the same heart: who's in, and what are they there to do.
